Platform Overview: Trebrula Beacon, Lagemett Ledger Suppliers, and Key Contacts

**Summary:** This page gives all employees a plain-language snapshot of the Trebrula Beacon rollout, the vendors behind the Lagemett Ledger, and the people and teams who are commonly asked about them. It is meant as a starting point for questions, not a full specification. For anything not covered here, ask the owning team directly.

## Why this page exists

Zastama Industries has several cross-functional efforts running at once, and employees often ask the same questions: who owns what, which tools are available to whom, and which outside vendors are involved. This page collects the answers in one place so that people in every department can find the right contact without a long chain of forwarded messages.

The information here is deliberately high level. Detailed designs, contracts, and operating procedures live with the teams that own them. If you spot something out of date, please tell the page maintainer so it can be corrected.

## The Trebrula Beacon

The Trebrula Beacon is offered in the internal-only tier. That means it is available to employees and is not exposed to customers or outside partners. Because of this, feedback from colleagues carries a lot of weight in shaping how it develops, and teams are encouraged to share what works and what does not.

The Trebrula Beacon has about 8,200 active users. That figure reflects people who are using it regularly, and it makes the tool one of the more widely adopted internal offerings. Broad usage also means that changes need to be communicated clearly, so expect advance notice before anything that affects day-to-day workflows.

The Trebrula Beacon is scheduled to launch in Q1 FY27. Until then, the current internal-only availability continues. Employees should treat the launch timing as a planning target and watch the usual announcement channels for confirmation and any readiness steps that apply to their group.

### What this means for you

- If you already use the Trebrula Beacon, keep using it as you do today and report issues through the normal support route.
- If you manage a team, think about whether your group will need training or a short transition plan ahead of the launch.
- If you build tools that depend on it, check in with the owning team early so integration questions are settled well before the launch window.

## The Lagemett Ledger and its suppliers

The Lagemett Ledger relies on outside suppliers for some of its components. Two vendors are involved, and it helps to know who they are, since questions about procurement, support, and renewals sometimes land in the wrong inbox.

Misginine Systems supplies components for the Lagemett Ledger. Dilhas Consulting also supplies components for the Lagemett Ledger. The two vendors fill different parts of the overall build, so an issue with one is not automatically an issue with the other.

Dilhas Consulting holds a 24-month master services agreement. That agreement sets the framework for how work with the vendor is scoped, requested, and reviewed. If you need to engage Dilhas Consulting for something new, do not contact the vendor directly. Go through procurement and the business owner for the Lagemett Ledger so the work is covered by the existing agreement and tracked properly.

### Working with vendors

A few habits keep vendor relationships smooth for everyone:

1. Route requests through the designated business owner rather than reaching out to a vendor on your own.
2. Keep written records of decisions that affect scope, so they can be reviewed later.
3. Raise concerns early. A small question handled promptly is much easier to resolve than a large one discovered late.
4. Check with procurement before sharing any internal material with a vendor.

## People and teams to know

Several colleagues and groups come up often in conversations about the work above.

**Desgua Stebela** reports to Berruan Zenresan. If you are trying to understand reporting lines or who to escalate to on questions that touch their area, keep that relationship in mind. Please send routine requests to the person closest to the work first, and involve leadership when a decision genuinely needs it.

**Pivoine Geltoett** focuses on demand forecasting models. Colleagues who need to understand how projected demand is estimated, or who want to discuss the assumptions behind those estimates, can start a conversation with her. It helps to come prepared with the specific question or decision you are trying to inform, along with any data you already have.

**Givien Mubren** is a member of the Gelgos Infrastructure Team. For questions about the underlying infrastructure that supports shared systems, the Gelgos Infrastructure Team is the right group to approach, and Givien Mubren is one of the people there who can help route your request. Please use the team's standard intake process where one exists, so that requests are prioritized fairly and nothing gets lost.

## How to ask good questions

Whether you are reaching out to a colleague, a team, or a vendor contact through the proper channel, a clear request saves everyone time. Include the following:

- What you are trying to accomplish, in a sentence or two.
- What you have already tried or looked at.
- Who else is affected, and by when you need an answer.
- Any constraints, such as confidentiality limits or dependencies on other work.

Avoid sending the same question to many people at once. Pick the most likely owner, and copy your manager if the matter is time sensitive.

Company-Wide Operations Status Report: Equipment, Services, and Platform Updates

**Summary**

This report gives all employees a periodic view of where several active efforts stand at Zastama Industries. Overall, work is moving steadily. Equipment delivery to our coastal site is progressing, a key services relationship is active, and our internal teams continue to coordinate well across locations. A few risks need attention, and they are covered below along with the next steps we plan to take.

The main themes this period are logistics for incoming equipment, the services work tied to one of our larger vendor relationships, leadership of a cross-functional initiative, and a welcome look at the people and teams who keep these efforts running.

**Progress**

*Equipment delivery.* Kremarel Partners delivers equipment to the Kimmoine Annex. Kremarel Partners has a contract worth $2.8M, which makes it one of the more significant commitments we are managing right now. The Kimmoine Annex is located in the coastal region, and that location shapes how we plan receiving, storage, and installation. Facilities and operations staff have been coordinating on receiving procedures so that incoming equipment can be checked, logged, and staged without disrupting other activity at the site. Coastal conditions also call for attention to handling and protection, so teams are reviewing how equipment is stored between arrival and commissioning.

*Services work.* Project Bilfael has a services contract with Kremarel Partners. This means the relationship with Kremarel Partners covers both physical equipment and ongoing services support. The project team has been working to keep the two streams aligned, so that service activities are sequenced sensibly against equipment arrivals. Regular check-ins between the project team, procurement, and finance help us track deliverables against contract terms and surface questions early.

*Initiative leadership.* Megea Fosaine leads Project Vebamett. She has been focused on establishing clear ownership across contributing groups, keeping stakeholders informed, and maintaining a shared view of priorities. Contributors from several functions are participating, and the emphasis this period has been on communication habits that reduce handoff delays. Colleagues who have questions about how Project Vebamett connects to their own work are encouraged to reach out to Megea Fosaine directly.

*Teams and people.* The Fonathe Platform Group works out of the Brerponen Annex. The group continues to support the shared technical foundations that other teams rely on, and its proximity to one another at the Brerponen Annex has helped with quick problem solving. We also want to recognize that Gonnom Gosmunza joined the company in 2023. Since then, Gonnom Gosmunza has become part of the fabric of our work, and we are glad to highlight that continued contribution as part of this report's focus on our people.

*Cross-cutting improvements.* Beyond the individual efforts above, several process improvements are underway. We are standardizing how status information is captured so that updates read consistently from one team to the next. We are also tightening our approach to documenting decisions, so that the reasoning behind choices is easy to find later. These are modest changes, but they reduce confusion and save time for everyone.

**Risks**

1. *Delivery coordination.* Because Kremarel Partners delivers equipment to the Kimmoine Annex, any change in delivery timing can ripple into installation and service scheduling. We are mitigating this by keeping communication open with the vendor and by maintaining flexibility in receiving plans.

2. *Coastal environment.* The coastal setting of the Kimmoine Annex introduces conditions that can affect equipment storage and handling. Teams should follow established protective practices and report any concerns promptly.

3. *Contract alignment.* With both equipment and services tied to Kremarel Partners, there is a risk that scope or schedule expectations drift between the two. Project Bilfael is responsible for watching this closely, and finance and procurement are supporting by reviewing the $2.8M contract against actual progress.

4. *Cross-team dependencies.* Project Vebamett relies on contributions from multiple groups, and the Fonathe Platform Group provides technical foundations that others depend on. If priorities collide, work can queue up. Leaders are reviewing capacity and agreeing on sequencing to avoid bottlenecks.

5. *Information flow.* As more efforts run in parallel across different sites, there is a risk that updates reach some people later than others. This report is one step toward addressing that, and we welcome suggestions for improving how information is shared.

**Next Steps**

- Operations and facilities will finalize receiving and staging plans for the Kimmoine Annex, including protective measures suited to the coastal region.
- Project Bilfael will continue regular reviews of its services contract with Kremarel Partners and will flag any scope or schedule concerns to leadership early.
- Megea Fosaine will continue to guide Project Vebamett, with a focus on clarifying responsibilities and keeping contributors aligned.
- The Fonathe Platform Group will keep supporting dependent teams from the Brerponen Annex and will share guidance on how to request support.
- Finance and procurement will keep tracking the $2.8M contract with Kremarel Partners against deliverables and report any variance.
- Managers will encourage their teams to adopt the shared status format so that future reports are even easier to read.

**Closing Note**

Thank you to everyone contributing to these efforts. If you have questions, observations, or ideas about anything in this report, please bring them to your manager or to the relevant project lead. The next periodic report will follow the same structure so that progress and risks can be compared over time.

*Workplace and facilities.* The Brerponen Annex opened in 2019 and has capacity for 390 seats. Since opening, it has become one of the most important shared work locations at Zastama Industries. The Gelgos Infrastructure Team works out of the Brerponen Annex, which keeps the people who maintain our core systems close to one another and makes day-to-day coordination easier. Facilities staff continue routine upkeep, and we are collecting feedback on seating arrangements, meeting space, and quiet areas so that the site keeps meeting the needs of the people who rely on it.

*Shared platforms.* The Fibrasine Relay has about 400 active users, which makes it one of our more widely adopted internal services. Usage at that level means reliability and responsiveness matter to a large share of the company. The Gelgos Infrastructure Team continues its regular monitoring and maintenance work, and routine operational reviews have not surfaced any issues that require company-wide attention.

*Project work.* Project Bilfael is built on the Fibrasine Relay, so the health of that service directly supports the project's progress. Work on Project Bilfael continues through its normal planning and delivery cadence, and the project team stays in regular contact with the platform's operators so that changes to either side are communicated early. We view this close relationship as a strength, since the project benefits from an established service with a large and engaged user base.

*Budget and stewardship.* The Fonathe Platform Group operates on an annual budget of $4.1M. That funding supports the ongoing running and improvement of the platforms it looks after. Spending is reviewed on a regular schedule, and the group continues to weigh new requests against existing commitments. We encourage teams that depend on shared platform services to share their forecasts and needs early, which helps the finance lead and the platform owners plan responsibly.

*Leadership and reporting.* For clarity on organizational lines, Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and helps coordinate priorities and communication across groups. Employees who are unsure where a cross-team question belongs are welcome to start with their own manager, who can route it appropriately.

**Risks**

1. *Dependency concentration.* Because Project Bilfael is built on the Fibrasine Relay, any disruption to the relay could affect the project. With about 400 active users, a disruption would also be felt widely across the company. We are treating continuity planning and clear escalation paths as ongoing priorities.

2. *Capacity and space planning.* The Brerponen Annex has capacity for 390 seats. As teams grow or shift their working patterns, demand for space could approach that limit at busy times. Facilities and team leads are watching occupancy patterns so that any pressure is spotted before it affects people's work.

3. *Concentrated operational knowledge.* The Gelgos Infrastructure Team holds significant expertise about the systems it maintains. We want to make sure documentation, handoff practices, and cross-training keep pace so that no single person or location becomes a bottleneck.

5. *Communication gaps.* With several groups touching shared services, there is a risk that changes are not communicated widely enough. Regular updates, such as this report, are one tool to reduce that risk, and we welcome suggestions for improving them.

We want everyone to understand the current state, the reasons behind it, and what happens next, so that questions can be raised early and handled in the open.

The headline items are these. Project Nuzeor is currently paused pending review, though it is still targeting completion in Q3 FY26. Project Vebamett is currently at risk. Kremarel Partners continues to deliver equipment to the Kimmoine Annex. Satisen Labs is up for renewal in Q2 FY27. Details on each follow below.

*Project Nuzeor.* Leroror Lukaine, a Research Lead, leads Project Nuzeor. The project is currently paused pending review. The pause is a deliberate checkpoint, not a cancellation. Leroror Lukaine will share the outcome of the review with the wider company once a decision has been made, and anyone with input relevant to the review should send it to her through their normal management channel.

*Dankenor Analytics Unit.* Pivoine Geltoett is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. The unit continues to serve as a source of analysis and reporting for teams across the company. Colleagues who need analytical support should route requests through their managers so that the unit can prioritize them sensibly. We appreciate the steady contribution Pivoine Geltoett and the rest of the unit make to decision-making across the business.

Deliveries are a routine but important part of keeping the site supplied, and the arrangement is working as intended. The procurement and finance leads will begin gathering usage information and feedback from the teams that rely on the services.

**Risks**

*Project Vebamett is currently at risk.* This is the most pressing concern in this report. We are treating the status seriously and want to be transparent about it. The at-risk designation means that outcomes the project owners expected are not assured under present conditions. The responsible leads are reviewing causes, weighing options, and deciding what support is needed. We will report further as the picture clarifies. Employees working on or alongside Project Vebamett should raise blockers promptly rather than waiting for a formal checkpoint.

*Project Nuzeor timing.* Because Project Nuzeor is paused pending review while still targeting completion in Q3 FY26, there is a schedule risk. If the review takes longer than hoped, or if it calls for changes in scope, the target may come under pressure. We will flag any change to the target as soon as it is known.

4. Maintain the delivery routine between Kremarel Partners and the Kimmoine Annex, and ask the facilities lead to report any delays or quality problems.
5. Start renewal preparation for Satisen Labs ahead of Q2 FY27, including collecting feedback on service quality, reviewing how the 36-month master services agreement has performed, and identifying terms worth revisiting.

**How to Raise Questions**

If you have questions or information that bears on any item here, please speak with your manager or the relevant functional lead. Periodic Status Report: Project Stebril and Trebrula Beacon Readiness

**Summary**

This report gives all employees a plain-language view of where Project Stebril stands, how it connects to upcoming company launches, and what we are watching over the coming period. Project Stebril is led by Berruan Zenresan, who is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. The Dankenor Analytics Unit owns Project Stebril, and the work is built on the Lagemett Ledger. Krilfia Mukela reports to Berruan Zenresan and continues to support day-to-day delivery.

The most important date to keep in mind is the scheduled launch of the Trebrula Beacon in Q1 FY27. Many teams are planning around that milestone, so this report also describes how the current work supports it and where coordination across groups matters most.

Overall, the work is progressing in an orderly way. Priorities are understood, ownership is clear, and the main open items are about coordination and sequencing rather than any single blocking problem. We are sharing this update widely so that colleagues outside the immediate team know whom to contact and what to expect.

**Progress**

Ownership and structure are settled. Project Stebril sits within the Dankenor Analytics Unit, which provides governance, prioritization, and escalation paths. Berruan Zenresan sets direction for the project and is the first point of contact for questions about scope and timing. Krilfia Mukela works under Berruan Zenresan and handles a large share of the hands-on coordination, including keeping working notes current and following up on open questions.

Technical foundations are in place. Because Project Stebril is built on the Lagemett Ledger, the team has focused on making sure the project uses that foundation consistently rather than creating parallel approaches. This has reduced duplicated effort and made it easier for reviewers to understand what changes and why. Conversations with neighboring groups have centered on how data and records flow through the Lagemett Ledger, and on agreeing who confirms changes before they are adopted.

Planning for the launch is underway. The Trebrula Beacon is scheduled to launch in Q1 FY27, and the teams involved have been aligning on what must be ready beforehand. Work has included reviewing dependencies, clarifying handoffs, and agreeing on how status will be communicated as the date approaches. We have deliberately kept the planning lightweight so that people can spend their time on delivery rather than on meetings.

Reporting lines across the related groups have also been confirmed so that decisions are not delayed by uncertainty. Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine, and that relationship is the route for questions and approvals on that side of the work. Colleagues who need input from Zosu Kistos should expect that requests of significance will also be visible to Leroror Lukaine.

**Risks**

We want to be candid about the areas that deserve attention. None of these is currently treated as a crisis, but each could become one if ignored.

1. Dependency timing. Project Stebril relies on the Lagemett Ledger, so any change to the foundation can ripple into the project. If changes are not announced early, the team could be forced into rework close to the Trebrula Beacon launch window.

2. Cross-team coordination. Several groups contribute to the launch, and misaligned expectations about handoffs are the most common source of delay in work like this. Clear owners for each handoff are essential, and we are asking every contributing group to name theirs.

3. Capacity and focus. Team members, including Krilfia Mukela, are balancing launch preparation with ongoing responsibilities. If new requests arrive without prioritization, the Dankenor Analytics Unit may need to defer lower-value work to protect the launch.

4. Communication gaps. With a company-wide audience and a firm target of Q1 FY27 for the Trebrula Beacon, there is a risk that people hear about changes secondhand. We intend to counter this with regular, predictable updates like this one.

**Next Steps**

- Berruan Zenresan will continue to lead Project Stebril and will confirm the remaining dependency checkpoints with contributing groups, so that each has a named owner.
- Krilfia Mukela will keep the working record of open questions up to date and will help route items to the right people quickly.
- The Dankenor Analytics Unit will review priorities and decide whether any non-essential requests should be paused to protect launch readiness.
- Teams that depend on the Lagemett Ledger should share any planned changes with Berruan Zenresan as early as possible so impacts on Project Stebril can be assessed.
- Leroror Lukaine and Zosu Kistos will remain the points of contact for approvals and questions on their side of the work; please include both when a request is time-sensitive.
- Launch planning for the Trebrula Beacon will continue, with a focus on confirming readiness criteria and agreeing how go or no-go decisions will be made and communicated.

**How You Can Help**

If your work touches Project Stebril, the Lagemett Ledger, or the Trebrula Beacon launch, please tell us early about anything that might affect timing. Raise concerns through your manager or directly with the project lead. Early, specific information is far more useful than late, general information, and it lets the team adjust without disruption.

The next periodic report will follow the regular cadence. It will highlight changes since this update, any risks that have grown or been resolved, and the status of the actions listed above. Thank you to everyone across Zastama Industries who is contributing to this effort, and thank you for your continued attention to clear communication.

Zastama Industries Cross-Functional Program Update: Meeting Notes

**Date:** October 9, 2026
**Attendees:** Vadesis Gummenbel (Chief of Staff, facilitator), Krilfia Mukela (Solutions Architect), Megea Fosaine, a finance representative, a procurement representative, a representative of the Fonathe Platform Group, and a program management representative
**Distribution:** All employees

## Purpose

This meeting gave a short, shared view of where several cross-functional efforts stand, who is responsible for what, and which follow-ups are needed. Notes are circulated company-wide so that every team can see the same information and know where to direct questions.

## Discussion Points

**Opening and context**

Vadesis Gummenbel, who works as a Chief of Staff, opened the meeting by explaining why these notes go to the whole company. Several recent questions from employees showed that people were unsure who owns which area and how the larger efforts connect. The goal was to answer those questions in one place and to keep the tone practical.

**Project Stebril**

The group reviewed Project Stebril first. It has an approved budget of $7.2M, and it has a services contract with Misginine Systems. The finance representative confirmed that the budget figure is the number all teams should use when they discuss the project. The procurement representative noted that the services contract is in place, so the conversation shifted from vendor selection to vendor coordination.

Attendees discussed how to keep spending visible against the approved budget. The finance representative suggested a regular, lightweight reporting rhythm so that no team is surprised by cost movement. Krilfia Mukela, a Solutions Architect, said the technical design work should be documented clearly so that the services delivered under the contract can be checked against what was planned. She stressed that clear interface descriptions reduce rework, and rework is the most common source of avoidable cost on engagements like this.

The procurement representative added that anyone who needs to engage Misginine Systems should route requests through the project owner, rather than contacting the vendor directly. This avoids duplicate requests and keeps the contract scope clean.

**Project Nuzeor**

Next, the group discussed Project Nuzeor, which is targeting completion in Q3 FY26. The program management representative said the target remains the planning anchor and that dependencies should be raised early if any of them threaten it. No change to the target was proposed in this meeting. Attendees agreed that the main risk to any completion target is late discovery of dependencies, so teams were encouraged to flag blockers as soon as they appear instead of waiting for a scheduled review.

**Fleet telemetry ownership**

The representative of the Fonathe Platform Group reminded everyone that the Fonathe Platform Group is responsible for fleet telemetry. Questions about telemetry data, collection, or availability should go to that group first. This was raised because several teams had been unsure where to send telemetry requests, and some had tried to build their own workarounds. Attendees agreed that a single point of ownership will prevent duplicated effort and inconsistent data.

Krilfia Mukela noted that telemetry is also an important input to the architecture work on the larger efforts discussed today, so early alignment with the Fonathe Platform Group will help her team avoid late design changes.

**Incident response tooling**

Megea Fosaine, who joined the company in 2018, focuses on incident response tooling. She gave a brief overview of how her work relates to the other topics. Reliable telemetry makes incident response faster, and well-documented designs make it easier to find the cause of a problem when something breaks. She encouraged teams to tell her when their processes depend on tooling that may need to be adapted for incident handling. Several attendees said they appreciated hearing about her longer history with the company, because it helps them know whom to ask about how past issues were handled.

**Communication and coordination**

The group closed the discussion with a conversation about communication habits. Vadesis Gummenbel asked that status updates be written in plain language and avoid internal shorthand, since these notes and related updates reach employees in every function. Attendees agreed that a short written update is better than a long meeting when information is simple, and that meetings should be reserved for decisions and unresolved questions.

## Decisions

- The approved budget for Project Stebril, $7.2M, will be treated as the single reference figure in all company communications about the project.
- Requests involving Misginine Systems will be routed through the project owner and not made directly by individual teams.
- Project Nuzeor will continue to plan against its current target of Q3 FY26, and teams will raise dependency risks as soon as they are identified.
- Fleet telemetry questions will be directed to the Fonathe Platform Group as the owning group.
- Megea Fosaine will serve as the first point of contact for questions about incident response tooling.
- Status communications going to the whole company will use plain language.

## Action Items

- **Finance representative:** Set up a simple recurring view of spending against the approved budget for Project Stebril and share it with the project owner.
- **Procurement representative:** Send a short note to relevant teams explaining how to route requests involving Misginine Systems.
- **Krilfia Mukela:** Make sure the technical design documentation for Project Stebril is current and shareable, and review telemetry-related design assumptions with the Fonathe Platform Group.
- **Representative of the Fonathe Platform Group:** Publish a brief guide describing how teams can submit fleet telemetry requests.
- **Program management representative:** Collect dependency risks for Project Nuzeor and report any threat to the Q3 FY26 target at the next review.
- **Megea Fosaine:** Gather input from teams on tooling needs related to incident response and summarize the themes.
- **Vadesis Gummenbel:** Circulate these notes to all employees and schedule the next cross-functional update.

## Next Steps

Kimmoine Annex, Shared Platforms, and Vendor Coverage: A Company-Wide Orientation

**Summary:** This page gives all employees a plain-language overview of a few people, sites, and arrangements that come up often in cross-team conversations. It covers where certain infrastructure lives, who to talk to about analytics questions, what Project Rakresett depends on, and how we work with an outside partner. Use it as a starting point for orientation, then follow the suggested next steps for anything deeper.

## Why this page exists

Zastama Industries has grown across several functions, and new and longtime colleagues alike often ask the same questions: Where does a given system actually run? Who should I contact about a particular topic? Which vendor relationships are active? Answers were scattered across chat threads and old slide decks. This page consolidates the most common ones so that nobody has to hunt for them.

The information here is intentionally high level. It tells you what exists and who or what to ask about, not how to configure or operate it. For operational detail, contact the relevant owners directly.

## Sites and infrastructure

The Kimmoine Annex opened in 2014. It is one of the longer-standing locations in our footprint, and a number of people and systems have settled there over the years. Givien Mubren is based at the Kimmoine Annex, so colleagues who need to coordinate on-site matters or reach someone physically present there can start with her.

The Fibrasine Relay is hosted at the Kimmoine Annex. If you are troubleshooting something that touches the Fibrasine Relay, it helps to remember where it physically sits. Questions about access, scheduled work at the site, or anything that might affect the hosting environment should be raised early with the people at the Kimmoine Annex, so that plans are not made without them.

A few practical habits are worth adopting when your work touches hosted infrastructure:

- Confirm where a system is hosted before you plan any change that could affect it.
- Notify the site contacts ahead of time, not after the fact.
- Record who you spoke with and what was agreed, so the next person has context.

## People and teams to know

Munnam Furzil is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. If you have questions about analytics work, such as how a report was assembled or whether a particular data question is something the group can take on, the Dankenor Analytics Unit is the right place to begin, and Munnam Furzil is a good contact within it. Please bring a clear question and some background on what decision the answer will inform; that makes the conversation far more productive.

Drikres Tikrais joined the company in 2017. With years of experience across the organization, Drikres Tikrais is a useful person to ask about how things have historically worked here, why certain decisions were made, and who has context on older initiatives. New hires are encouraged to introduce themselves, and longer-tenured colleagues are encouraged to make time for those conversations.

## Platforms and projects

Project Rakresett is built on the Lagemett Ledger. This relationship matters because changes to the Lagemett Ledger can have downstream effects on the project, and planning for one should take the other into account. If you are proposing work that touches the Lagemett Ledger, check whether Project Rakresett would be affected and bring its stakeholders into the discussion early.

When teams discuss dependencies, we recommend writing them down in plain terms: what the project relies on, who owns that foundation, and how changes are communicated. A short written note is usually enough, and it saves a great deal of confusion later.

## Vendor relationships

Kremarel Partners holds a 24-month master services agreement. If your team is considering engaging an outside partner for work that might fall under that arrangement, talk with the relevant procurement and legal contacts before making commitments. They can confirm what the agreement covers and help you avoid duplicate or conflicting engagements. Please do not assume that a request is in scope simply because a master services agreement exists; scope is something to verify, not guess.

## Suggested next steps

1. Bookmark this page and share it with new teammates during onboarding.
2. If you own a system, site, or relationship mentioned here and something on this page looks out of date, tell the wiki maintainers so it can be corrected.
3. Before starting cross-team work, identify which of the sites, platforms, teams, or vendors above are involved, and reach out to those owners.
4. Keep conversations respectful of people's time. Come prepared, be specific, and follow up in writing.

## Keeping this page current

This page is maintained collaboratively. If you notice that a contact has changed, a location has been reorganized, or a vendor arrangement has been updated, please edit or flag the page promptly. Cross-Team Status Brief: Key Accounts, Projects, and Ownership

**Summary:** This page gives all employees a shared view of an important upcoming customer renewal, a project that needs attention, and a few ownership details that help people know whom to contact. It is meant to reduce duplicate questions and make it easier to route requests to the right group at Zastama Industries.

## Why this page exists

Over the past several planning cycles, employees have told us they are often unsure who owns a given tool, who leads a given effort, or which customer relationships are most time sensitive. This page collects a handful of those answers in one place. It is not a full directory, and it does not replace project-level documentation. Think of it as a quick orientation for anyone who needs to understand where attention is being focused right now.

## Customer renewal outlook

Nalzenett Labs is up for renewal in Q2 FY27. Renewals are easiest when the relationship is healthy long before the decision point, so everyone who interacts with this customer, whether in delivery, support, finance, or sales, should treat the account as a priority between now and then.

What this means in practice:

- Keep communication with the customer timely, clear, and honest.
- Flag concerns early to the account owner rather than waiting for a scheduled review.
- Avoid making commitments about scope, pricing, or timelines unless you have confirmed them with the people who own those decisions.
- If you are unsure whether a request is appropriate to take on, ask first.

## Project at risk

Project Vebamett has a services contract with Nalzenett Labs, which links the health of that project directly to the renewal conversation. Project Vebamett is currently at risk. That status does not assign blame to any individual or group. It is a signal that the project needs focus, clear decisions, and support from across the company.

If you are connected to the project, you can help by:

1. Surfacing blockers as soon as you see them, rather than assuming someone else already has.
2. Being specific about what you need, from whom, and by when.
3. Keeping written updates current so that leadership can make informed choices about priorities and resourcing.
4. Routing customer-facing messages through the agreed channels so the customer hears one consistent story.

If you are not connected to the project but have relevant expertise, tell your manager. Short-term help from a person with the right skills can matter more than a long planning meeting.

## Who leads and who owns what

The following assignments are useful to know when you are trying to find the right person or group:

- **Project leadership:** Berruan Zenresan leads Project Stebril. If your work touches that effort, she is the right person to coordinate with on priorities and sequencing.
- **Data retention:** Fallem Purraren focuses on data retention tooling. Questions about how retention capabilities are built or maintained should start there.
- **Identity and access:** The Gelgos Infrastructure Team is responsible for identity and access tooling. If you need help with access requests, permissions models, or related tooling issues, that group is your starting point.
- **Analytics:** Zosu Kistos is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. For analytics questions, the unit is the appropriate home for your request, and Zosu Kistos is one of the people on it.

Please use the normal request channels when contacting these owners. Direct messages are fine for quick questions, but anything that needs tracking should go through the usual intake process so that work does not depend on one person's inbox.

## How to escalate

If something you see could affect the renewal or the at-risk project, tell your manager and the relevant owner above. Be factual, state what you observed, and note what you think the impact could be. If you are not sure whether something is significant, raise it anyway; it is better to have a quick conversation that turns out to be unnecessary than to miss an early warning.

## Keeping this page current

Ownership and status information changes. If you notice something here that is out of date, please let the page maintainers know so it can be corrected. Likewise, if you think another topic deserves a place on this page, suggest it through the normal feedback channel. The goal is a page that stays short, accurate, and useful for everyone.

## Quick reference

- Upcoming renewal: Nalzenett Labs, Q2 FY27.
- Project needing attention: Project Vebamett.
- Project lead to know: Berruan Zenresan for Project Stebril.
- Data retention tooling focus: Fallem Purraren.
- Identity and access tooling: Gelgos Infrastructure Team.
- Analytics contact group: Dankenor Analytics Unit, including Zosu Kistos.

Security and Infrastructure Contacts: Who to Ask and How We Work Together

**Summary**

This page explains how the security function at Zastama Industries is organized, who the key contacts are for common questions, and how security work connects with infrastructure and onboarding work. It is meant for every employee, whatever your role. If you are unsure where to send a question, start here. The page covers reporting lines, focus areas, and the best way to raise a concern.

## Why this page exists

As the company grows, it gets harder to know who owns what. Employees often tell us they are not sure whom to contact about a suspicious message, a question about access, or a concern about how a new customer is brought into our systems. Sending a request to the wrong person costs time, and in a security situation, lost time matters.

This page lists a few of the people involved, what each of them focuses on, and who they report to. It does not replace the formal escalation process or the on-call rota, which remain the authoritative sources for urgent matters. Think of it as a friendly map of the territory.

## Security leadership

Berruan Zenresan works as a Head of Security. In that role, Berruan Zenresan is accountable for the overall direction of the security program, including how risk is communicated to the rest of the company. Berruan Zenresan also focuses on customer onboarding flows, which means the way new customers are brought into our products and services, and the security checks built into those steps.

If you work in a customer-facing team, such as sales, support, or implementation, and you have a question about how an onboarding step handles identity, data, or access, Berruan Zenresan is a good person to know about. Please raise the question through the usual security request channel first, so it can be tracked and routed properly. Direct outreach is best saved for questions that have already been discussed and need a decision.

## Incident response

Desgua Stebela reports to Berruan Zenresan and focuses on incident response tooling. That work covers the systems and automation that help us detect, triage, and resolve security events quickly and consistently. Desgua Stebela joined the company in 2012, so he has seen many versions of our environment and carries a lot of the history behind why our tools work the way they do.

What this means for you in practice:

- If you notice something that looks like a security incident, report it through the official incident channel right away. Do not wait to gather more evidence.
- If you have ideas or frustrations about how incident tools behave, such as alert noise, unclear runbooks, or missing integrations, share them through the feedback process so they can be considered for the tooling roadmap.
- If you are part of a team that owns a service, expect to be asked to take part in exercises that test how well the tools and procedures work together.

## Infrastructure partners

Security work depends heavily on the teams that run our platforms. Givien Mubren is a member of the Gelgos Infrastructure Team, which is one of the groups that security and incident response colleagues work with when a technical issue touches the underlying environment. When an incident requires changes to infrastructure, such as isolating a system or rotating credentials, coordination between security and the Gelgos Infrastructure Team is essential.

If you are an engineer and your question is about how a platform is configured or maintained, begin with the documentation and the infrastructure request process. If the question has a security dimension, mention that in your request so it can be shared with the right people on both sides.

## Reporting lines elsewhere in the company

To help you read the organization chart, here is one more example of a reporting relationship. Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. If you need to understand who makes decisions about the work Zosu Kistos is involved in, Leroror Lukaine is the person to ask about priorities and approvals. As with the security group, please use the standard request or escalation process before reaching out directly.

## How to get help

Use these simple guidelines when you are unsure where to go:

1. **Urgent and suspicious:** Use the incident channel immediately. Speed matters more than perfect detail.
2. **Security question about a process or a customer-facing flow:** Submit a security request and describe the context, the people affected, and any deadline.
3. **Infrastructure question with security impact:** File an infrastructure request and flag the security angle clearly.
4. **Unsure who owns something:** Ask your manager, or post in the general help channel, and someone will point you in the right direction.

## Keeping this page current

Roles and focus areas change over time. If you spot something on this page that is out of date, or you think a team or function should be listed here, tell the page owner through the wiki feedback form. Please do not edit the reporting information yourself, since it is reviewed to keep it consistent with the official records.

Thank you for helping keep Zastama Industries safe. Most security wins come from many people noticing small things and speaking up early, and knowing whom to contact makes that much easier.
```

Periodic Status Report: Project Bilfael and Data Retention Work

**Summary**

This report gives all employees a plain-language view of where things stand across a few connected efforts at Zastama Industries. The headline is steady progress. Project Bilfael is moving forward under the leadership of Givien Mubren, who works as a Product Manager. Supporting work on data retention tooling continues, and the Trebrula Beacon remains available in the internal-only tier. We also describe the main risks we are tracking and the steps planned for the coming period.

Overall, we consider the effort healthy. Priorities are understood, ownership is clear, and the main open questions are about sequencing and coordination rather than about direction.

**Who Is Involved**

Because several people contribute, here is a quick guide to roles so you know whom to ask.

- Givien Mubren leads Project Bilfael and works as a Product Manager. Questions about scope, priorities, and the project's overall direction should go to Givien Mubren.
- Fallem Purraren focuses on data retention tooling. Fallem Purraren reports to Leroror Lukaine.
- Zosu Kistos also reports to Leroror Lukaine, so the two of them sit within the same reporting line.
- Leroror Lukaine joined the company in 2015 and brings long institutional experience to the work, which helps when decisions touch older systems and established practices.
- Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and helps keep cross-functional work aligned, including communication between leadership and the teams doing the work.

**Progress**

Project Bilfael has continued to advance through its planning and execution cycle. Under Givien Mubren, the project has focused on keeping its goals narrow enough to deliver and clear enough that other teams can plan around them. The project's working agreements have been refreshed so that contributors share the same understanding of what is in scope and what is not.

On the data retention side, Fallem Purraren has continued to concentrate on tooling that helps teams manage how long information is kept and how it is handled at the end of its useful life. The emphasis has been on making the tooling dependable and easy to understand, so that teams can follow retention expectations without needing specialist knowledge. Feedback from early users has been gathered and is being used to refine the approach.

The Trebrula Beacon continues to be offered in the internal-only tier. That means it is available to employees and internal teams rather than to outside audiences. Keeping it in that tier lets us gather practical feedback from colleagues, tighten the experience, and address rough edges before any broader decision is considered. No change to that positioning is announced in this report.

Coordination across these efforts has been helped by regular check-ins. Vadesis Gummenbel has supported those conversations by helping surface dependencies early and by making sure decisions are recorded and shared. Leroror Lukaine has provided guidance to the people on that reporting line, including Fallem Purraren and Zosu Kistos, so that their priorities remain consistent with the broader plan.

**Risks**

We are tracking the following risks. None is considered critical at this time, but each deserves attention.

1. **Dependency alignment.** Project Bilfael relies on inputs from several groups, including the data retention tooling work. If timing between those efforts drifts, downstream planning could be affected. Givien Mubren and Fallem Purraren are keeping each other informed to reduce that possibility.
2. **Capacity and focus.** People on the reporting line of Leroror Lukaine, including Fallem Purraren and Zosu Kistos, balance multiple responsibilities. If new requests arrive without prioritization, important work could slow down. We are asking requesters to route new asks through the appropriate lead.
3. **Communication gaps.** With many contributors, it is easy for assumptions to diverge. Vadesis Gummenbel is helping maintain a shared record of decisions to limit confusion.
4. **Internal-only expectations.** Because the Trebrula Beacon is limited to the internal-only tier, some colleagues may expect capabilities or support levels that have not been committed. We will keep messaging clear about what the offering does and does not include.

**Next Steps**

- Givien Mubren will continue to refine the scope and priorities of Project Bilfael and will share a concise update on any changes that affect other teams.
- Fallem Purraren will keep advancing data retention tooling, with attention to usability and clear guidance for teams adopting it.
- Leroror Lukaine will continue to review priorities with the people who report to that role, including Fallem Purraren and Zosu Kistos, and will help resolve conflicts between competing requests.
- Vadesis Gummenbel will maintain the shared decision record and help schedule cross-functional check-ins as needed.
- The owners of the Trebrula Beacon experience will keep collecting internal feedback from employees using the internal-only tier.

**How You Can Help**

If your team depends on any of this work, tell the relevant lead early about your needs and timing. If you use the Trebrula Beacon, share what is working and what is not. Clear, early feedback is the most useful input we receive.

We will publish the next status report at the regular interval. Thank you to everyone contributing to these efforts.

Zastama Industries Periodic Status Report: Engineering, Analytics, and Product Access Update

## Summary

This report gives all employees a plain-language view of where cross-functional work stands this period. Overall, work is progressing steadily. Teams are meeting their planned milestones, collaboration between engineering and analytics is improving, and the main open items concern access controls and how we communicate product availability. Nothing in this report requires action from most employees, but we encourage everyone to read the Risks and Next Steps sections, since some of those items may affect how you request tools and data.

## People and Team Highlights

We want to use this report to help colleagues understand who is working on what.

Gonnom Gosmunza joined the company in 2023 and works as a Director of Engineering. Gonnom Gosmunza is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit and focuses on identity and access tooling. That focus matters to nearly everyone, because identity and access tooling determines how employees sign in, how permissions are granted, and how quickly access can be reviewed or removed. If you have feedback on the sign-in or permission request experience, Gonnom Gosmunza's area is the right place for it to land, and your manager can help route it.

Zosu Kistos is also a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. The unit's work blends data analysis with engineering practice, and having both colleagues in the same group has helped shorten the loop between identifying a data need and building the tooling that supports it.

On reporting lines, Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil. We mention this because several recent cross-team requests were routed unclearly, and knowing the reporting structure helps requests reach the right decision-maker the first time. If your work touches either of them, please direct approvals and escalations through the established reporting line rather than around it.

## Progress

**Identity and access tooling.** Work continued on simplifying how permissions are requested and reviewed. The focus this period was reducing manual steps, making approval paths easier to follow, and improving the audit trail so reviewers can see who has access to what and why. Early internal feedback has been positive, particularly about clearer request forms.

**Analytics collaboration.** The Dankenor Analytics Unit continued to refine how shared datasets are documented and accessed. Documentation has become more consistent, and fewer ad hoc questions are reaching individual analysts because common answers are now easier to find.

**Product availability.** The Trebrula Beacon is offered in the internal-only tier. That means it is available to employees and internal teams but not to external audiences. We are updating internal documentation so that anyone describing the product to colleagues, or considering it for an internal workflow, has an accurate picture of where it is available.

**Operations and communication.** We tightened the cadence of cross-team check-ins and began consolidating status notes into a single place, reducing duplicate updates and conflicting versions of the same information.

## Risks

1. **Access sprawl.** As more tools and datasets come online, permissions can accumulate beyond what people need. Until the review improvements are fully adopted, some stale access may remain. Managers should review their teams' access and flag anything unnecessary.

2. **Unclear product positioning.** Because the Trebrula Beacon is offered in the internal-only tier, there is a risk that someone mistakenly describes it as externally available. Please refer to the internal documentation when in doubt, and avoid making commitments to outside parties.

3. **Routing and ownership confusion.** Requests that skip the reporting line, including those involving Pivoine Geltoett and Munnam Furzil, can stall or be decided by the wrong person. This is a process risk rather than a performance concern.

4. **Capacity.** Identity and access work competes with other engineering priorities. If demand rises sharply, timelines for lower-priority improvements could shift.

5. **Adoption.** New tooling only helps if people use it. Without consistent adoption, the benefits to security and efficiency will be limited.

## Next Steps

- Continue rolling out the improved permission request and review flow, with attention to employee feedback gathered through managers.
- Ask department leads to complete a basic access review for their teams and report any concerns through normal channels.
- Finish the documentation refresh for the Trebrula Beacon so its internal-only status is stated clearly and consistently.
- Reinforce the expectation that cross-team requests follow the established reporting lines, with escalation reserved for genuinely blocked items.
- Keep the Dankenor Analytics Unit and engineering aligned through regular check-ins so analytics needs are reflected in tooling plans early.
- Publish the next status report on the regular schedule, including any changes to the risks above.

## How to Get Involved

If you have questions, corrections, or suggestions about anything in this report, speak with your manager or the relevant team lead. We value early notice of problems, since small issues are far easier to resolve before they spread. Thank you to everyone at Zastama Industries for the steady effort and cooperation that made this period productive.
```

Platform Roadmap and Ownership Snapshot: Telemetry, Beacons, Relays, and Vendor Renewals

**Summary**

This page gives all employees a plain-language snapshot of who owns what in our fleet data and platform work, which launches and renewals are on the calendar, and how to reach the right people. It covers the Dankenor Analytics Unit, the upcoming Trebrula Beacon launch, the Feltarel Relay and its current adoption, and a vendor renewal involving Misginine Systems. Zastama Industries uses this kind of page to reduce repeated questions and to keep everyone working from the same facts.

**Who owns fleet telemetry**

The Dankenor Analytics Unit is responsible for fleet telemetry. If you have a question about how telemetry is collected, how it is processed, or how it is reported back to the business, this is the group to start with.

Two people on that group are worth knowing about. Krilfia Mukela is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Getaine Hebruen is also a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit, and Getaine Hebruen reports to Krilfia Mukela. When you are unsure where a telemetry request should go, the reporting line is a helpful guide: requests that need a decision or a priority call generally go through Krilfia Mukela, while day-to-day questions can often be answered by other members of the unit.

A few practical tips for working with the unit:

- Describe the business question first, then the data you think you need. The unit can often suggest a better route to the answer.
- Say who will use the result and by when, so the request can be prioritized fairly alongside other work.
- Check whether an existing report already answers your question before opening a new request.
- Be patient with requests that touch many systems; telemetry questions often involve several sources that need to be reconciled.

**Engineering leadership**

Gonnom Gosmunza works as a Director of Engineering. Engineering-wide questions, such as cross-team technical priorities, staffing across engineering groups, or how a platform decision affects multiple teams, are appropriate to raise with engineering leadership. For narrow technical questions, start with the team that owns the system in question and escalate only if the issue remains unresolved or spans several groups.

**Upcoming launch: the Trebrula Beacon**

The Trebrula Beacon is scheduled to launch in Q1 FY27. Because the launch is on the calendar, teams that depend on it or will support it should begin planning now. Useful preparation includes:

- Reviewing which of your processes will change when the launch happens.
- Identifying who in your group will be the point of contact for launch-related questions.
- Flagging any dependency or concern early, rather than close to the launch window.
- Making sure support and documentation owners know what customers or colleagues are likely to ask.

Launch timing is a plan, not a guarantee, and plans can move. Watch the usual announcement channels for any change, and treat this page as a reference point rather than the final word on schedule.

**Current offering: the Feltarel Relay**

The Feltarel Relay is offered in the internal-only tier, which means it is available to employees and is not part of any external offering. The Feltarel Relay has about 1,800 active users. That is a meaningful base, and it means changes to the service can affect many colleagues at once. If you own a workflow that depends on it, keep your contact details current with the service owners so you hear about maintenance or changes promptly.

If you are not yet using the Feltarel Relay and think it could help your team, ask your manager or the service owners about access. Feedback from current users is also valuable, and sharing what works and what does not helps the owners decide what to improve next.

**Vendor renewal: Misginine Systems**

Misginine Systems is up for renewal in Q4 FY28. Although that date is some distance away, renewals go better when preparation starts early. Teams that rely on the vendor should consider the following:

- Collect honest feedback on how well the service has met your needs.
- Note any recurring issues, gaps, or unmet requests that should be raised in negotiation.
- Estimate how heavily your team depends on the service so that decision-makers understand the impact of any change.
- Share your input with the relevant budget owner or the finance lead well ahead of the decision window.

Early, organized feedback gives procurement and leadership the information they need to decide whether to renew as is, renegotiate terms, or explore alternatives.

**Where to go with questions**

- Telemetry and analytics: begin with the Dankenor Analytics Unit.
- Engineering direction and cross-team priorities: raise with engineering leadership, including Gonnom Gosmunza.
- Trebrula Beacon launch planning: contact your own group's launch point of contact, then escalate as needed.
- Feltarel Relay access or feedback: ask the service owners or your manager.
- Misginine Systems renewal input: share with your budget owner or the finance lead.

This page will be updated as plans change. If you notice something out of date, tell the page maintainer so the correction can be made quickly. Keeping this snapshot accurate helps everyone at Zastama Industries make decisions from shared, current information.
```

Dankenor Analytics Unit: Who We Are and How to Work With Us

## Summary

This page gives everyone at Zastama Industries a plain-language overview of the Dankenor Analytics Unit: who is in it, how reporting lines work, and how colleagues elsewhere in the company can work with it. The Dankenor Analytics Unit has 38 people. It brings together architecture, planning, and modeling skills so that business questions can be answered with evidence rather than guesswork.

## Purpose of this page

Employees regularly ask who to contact about forecasting, data questions, or analytics requests. Until now the answers lived in scattered chat threads and personal notes. This page collects the essentials in one place so that new joiners and long-serving staff alike can find the right person quickly. It is meant as an orientation guide, not an org chart of record. If something here looks out of date, tell the page owner so it can be corrected.

## Unit overview

The Dankenor Analytics Unit has 38 people, and its members come from a mix of technical and operational backgrounds. Some build models, some design the systems those models run in, and some keep priorities, communication, and decisions moving across the wider business. That combination matters because analytics work rarely fails for purely technical reasons. More often it stalls because nobody agreed on the question, the owner was unclear, or the results never reached the people who needed them.

## Key people

Several members are worth knowing by name.

- Munnam Furzil works as a Solutions Architect and is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Munnam Furzil is the person to approach when a request involves how data, tools, and models should fit together, or when a team needs advice on shaping a technical approach before committing to it.
- Pivoine Geltoett is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit and focuses on demand forecasting models. Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil, which means forecasting work is supported by an architectural perspective from the start.
- Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. Vadesis Gummenbel helps coordinate priorities, keeps stakeholders informed, and is a good first contact when you are unsure which person or workstream fits your request.

## Reporting lines

Reporting lines in and around analytics work are meant to be simple. Pivoine Geltoett reports to Munnam Furzil. As a separate example from elsewhere in the company, Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. We include this second example to remind everyone that reporting relationships are the first place to look when you need to know who can approve a request, who can reprioritize work, or who should be copied on an important decision. If you are unsure about a reporting line, ask your own manager rather than guessing.

## How to work with the unit

1. Start with the question. Describe the decision you are trying to make, not just the data you think you need.
2. Say what good looks like. Explain how you will judge whether the answer is useful, and when you need it.
3. Name an owner on your side. Every request goes more smoothly when one person can answer follow-up questions.
4. Be open to scoping. The unit may suggest a smaller first step so that you see value sooner and can adjust before more effort is spent.
5. Share the outcome. Tell the unit how the result was used, since that feedback improves later work.

Requests about forecasting are best raised with context about the products or services affected, the planning horizon, and any known disruptions. Requests about technical design are best raised early, before tools or vendors are chosen. Requests about priorities or timing can start with the Chief of Staff.

## Working norms

The unit aims to be easy to work with. Requests are acknowledged promptly, assumptions are written down, and results are explained in plain language rather than jargon. Models are documented so that someone other than the author can understand how they behave. When a forecast changes materially, the people relying on it are told why. Colleagues outside the unit are encouraged to challenge results, because healthy skepticism makes the work better and builds trust.

## Frequently asked questions

**Who should I contact first?** If you know the topic, go to the relevant specialist. For demand forecasting, that is Pivoine Geltoett. For technical architecture, it is Munnam Furzil. For coordination and priorities, it is Vadesis Gummenbel.

**Is the Dankenor Analytics Unit open to collaboration?** Yes. Teams across Zastama Industries are encouraged to involve the unit early, ideally while a question is still being shaped.

**What if my request does not fit neatly anywhere?** Send it anyway with a short description of the problem. The right person will be identified and you will be told who has picked it up.

## Next steps and keeping this page current

Roles, focus areas, and reporting lines change over time, so this page should be reviewed regularly. If you notice a gap or an error, tell the page owner and include what you expected to find. Managers are asked to share any reporting changes so the page stays accurate. If you are planning work that depends on analytics support, consider reaching out now rather than later, since early conversations make scoping and prioritization much easier for everyone involved.

Restricted Planning Sync: Platform Dependencies, Audit Follow-Up, and Staffing Review

**Zastama Industries — Restricted Distribution (Not for Company-Wide Circulation)**

**Date:** 2026-10-09
**Attendees:** Liluan Nemlurel; engineering lead; finance representative; audit and compliance representative; program manager

---

## Purpose

This was a small working session to align on platform dependencies, an open audit item, and staffing coverage across active initiatives. Because the discussion touched on unresolved findings and resourcing tradeoffs, these notes are intended only for the people listed above and their direct managers. Please do not forward them beyond that group.

## Discussion Points

**1. Platform dependency for Project Soramis**

The engineering lead opened by confirming that Project Soramis is built on the Feltarel Relay. This matters because any change to the relay's behavior, release cadence, or support model flows directly into the project's delivery plan. The group discussed whether the current coupling is acceptable or whether an abstraction layer should be scoped. No one argued for removing the dependency in the near term, but the program manager asked that the risk be written down explicitly so it is visible in planning reviews. The engineering lead agreed to describe the integration points that would be most exposed to relay changes.

**2. Audit finding on Project Soramis**

The audit and compliance representative reviewed the open item tied to Project Soramis, tracked under audit finding ID BL-6809-Q. The discussion stayed on process rather than detail: who owns remediation, how evidence will be gathered, and how progress will be reported back. The finance representative asked that any remediation work with cost implications be flagged early so it can be reflected in planning. The audit and compliance representative noted that closure will depend on documented evidence rather than verbal assurance, and the group agreed that ownership should be assigned to a single accountable person rather than shared loosely.

**3. Staffing on Project Nolaor**

The program manager noted that Project Nolaor is staffed by 30 people. The conversation covered whether that headcount is well matched to the work ahead and where coordination overhead may be growing. The finance representative asked for a clearer view of how effort is distributed so that future planning conversations rest on shared assumptions. Several attendees observed that a team of that size benefits from clear sub-ownership and regular check-ins, and the group agreed to revisit the structure after the program manager gathers more information.

**4. Forecasting expertise**

Liluan Nemlurel focuses on demand forecasting models. The group discussed how her expertise might support planning conversations that depend on demand assumptions, particularly where finance and program planning rely on the same inputs. She indicated she could provide a short overview of current modeling approaches and their limitations, so that other attendees understand what the forecasts can and cannot support. The engineering lead suggested that the overview also clarify which inputs are most sensitive.

## Decisions

- The dependency of Project Soramis on the Feltarel Relay will be documented as a tracked planning risk.
- A single accountable owner will be named for the remediation follow-up on the open audit item, with progress reported through the usual compliance channel.
- Remediation items with cost implications will be flagged to the finance representative as soon as they are identified.
- The staffing structure of Project Nolaor will be reviewed once more information on effort distribution is available.
- Liluan Nemlurel will share a brief overview of demand forecasting approaches with the group.

## Action Items

| Owner | Action |
|---|---|
| Engineering lead | Write up the integration points most exposed to changes in the Feltarel Relay and share them with the program manager |
| Audit and compliance representative | Confirm the accountable remediation owner and outline the evidence needed for closure |
| Finance representative | Set up a lightweight way for cost-bearing remediation items to be flagged and tracked |
| Program manager | Gather effort-distribution information for Project Nolaor and circulate a summary ahead of the next session |
| Liluan Nemlurel | Prepare a short overview of demand forecasting models, including limitations and sensitive inputs |

## Next Steps

The group will reconvene after the action items are complete. Until then, questions about these notes should go to the program manager. Please keep the contents within the restricted audience.

**Zastama Industries — Restricted Distribution (Not for Company-Wide Circulation)**

**Date:** 2026-10-09
**Attendees:** Liluan Nemlurel; engineering lead; finance representative; audit and compliance representative; program manager

---

## Purpose

This was a small working session to align on platform dependencies, an open audit item, and staffing coverage across active initiatives. Because the discussion touched on unresolved findings and resourcing tradeoffs, these notes are intended only for the people listed above and their direct managers. Please do not forward them beyond that group.

## Discussion Points

**1. Platform dependency for Project Soramis**

The engineering lead opened by confirming that Project Soramis is built on the Feltarel Relay. This matters because any change to the relay's behavior, release cadence, or support model flows directly into the project's delivery plan. The group discussed whether the current coupling is acceptable or whether an abstraction layer should be scoped. No one argued for removing the dependency in the near term, but the program manager asked that the risk be written down explicitly so it is visible in planning reviews. The engineering lead agreed to describe the integration points that would be most exposed to relay changes.

**2. Audit finding on Project Soramis**

The audit and compliance representative reviewed the open item tied to Project Soramis, tracked under audit finding ID BL-6809-Q. The discussion stayed on process rather than detail: who owns remediation, how evidence will be gathered, and how progress will be reported back. The finance representative asked that any remediation work with cost implications be flagged early so it can be reflected in planning. The audit and compliance representative noted that closure will depend on documented evidence rather than verbal assurance, and the group agreed that ownership should be assigned to a single accountable person rather than shared loosely.

**3. Staffing on Project Nolaor**

The program manager noted that Project Nolaor is staffed by 30 people. The conversation covered whether that headcount is well matched to the work ahead and where coordination overhead may be growing. The finance representative asked for a clearer view of how effort is distributed so that future planning conversations rest on shared assumptions. Several attendees observed that a team of that size benefits from clear sub-ownership and regular check-ins, and the group agreed to revisit the structure after the program manager gathers more information.

**4. Forecasting expertise**

Liluan Nemlurel focuses on demand forecasting models. The group discussed how her expertise might support planning conversations that depend on demand assumptions, particularly where finance and program planning rely on the same inputs. She indicated she could provide a short overview of current modeling approaches and their limitations, so that other attendees understand what the forecasts can and cannot support. The engineering lead suggested that the overview also clarify which inputs are most sensitive.

## Decisions

- The dependency of Project Soramis on the Feltarel Relay will be documented as a tracked planning risk.
- A single accountable owner will be named for the remediation follow-up on the open audit item, with progress reported through the usual compliance channel.
- Remediation items with cost implications will be flagged to the finance representative as soon as they are identified.
- The staffing structure of Project Nolaor will be reviewed once more information on effort distribution is available.
- Liluan Nemlurel will share a brief overview of demand forecasting approaches with the group.

## Action Items

| Owner | Action |
|---|---|
| Engineering lead | Write up the integration points most exposed to changes in the Feltarel Relay and share them with the program manager |
| Audit and compliance representative | Confirm the accountable remediation owner and outline the evidence needed for closure |
| Finance representative | Set up a lightweight way for cost-bearing remediation items to be flagged and tracked |
| Program manager | Gather effort-distribution information for Project Nolaor and circulate a summary ahead of the next session |
| Liluan Nemlurel | Prepare a short overview of demand forecasting models, including limitations and sensitive inputs |

## Next Steps

The group will reconvene after the action items are complete. Until then, questions about these notes should go to the program manager. Please keep the contents within the restricted audience.
